A.evidence:
I confirmed this myself in CYBER.BIN (base 0x0600D000) and local/opt001/wramh_27173.bin. A is the unused tail of the VDP1 command-list buffer. A's lower edge is only the highest point the list has reached so far.

(1) The buffer. Its base is *0x06047D1C = 0x060E1000 and the write pointer is 0x060CE668. The next buffer starts at *0x06047D20 = 0x060E8000, so the list's only real upper limit is 0x060E8000, which is A's end. The text appender 0x060112DC-0x06011328 stores a 32-byte command at *0x060CE668, then does `add #32,r3; mov.l r3,@r7` with no compare against any limit. The string routine 0x06011344-0x06011398 calls it once per character above 0x20 until it reaches NUL, so a longer string means more commands.

(2) The flush. Code at 0x0600FF7C-0x0600FF8E computes r14 = *0x060CE668 - *0x06047D1C and calls 0x0603D22C(r4=0x25C00000, r5=0x060E1000, r6=r14). For this source and destination, 0x0603D22C takes the SCU-DMA path: it sets up through 0x06040D78 and starts through 0x06040DD8 (0x0603D2A4-0x0603D30C). Code at 0x0600FF90-0x0600FF98 then keeps the largest size in 0x06047D30.

(3) The proof. In wramh_27173.bin, *0x06047D30 = 0x00002300, and the end command 80 00 00 00 is at 0x060E32E0, the last non-zero byte of the buffer. So at least one frame transferred 0x060E1000-0x060E32FF, and the SCU DMA read A's first 28 bytes, 0x060E32E4-0x060E32FF. Master-SH-2 breakpoints cannot see an SCU-DMA read, and the 0xA5 canary only catches writes.

(4) The boundary. The EXP-0064 census found the highest byte that ever changed to be the end command's long at 0x060E32E0-0x060E32E3. That is exactly where A's start of 0x060E32E4 comes from, so the start is an observed maximum and not a structural limit. In the other 18 dumps the maximum was smaller, from 0xA20 to 0x13E0, so the busiest frame on record came from the boot/attract/title/Options session.

(5) Risk. A frame with more than about 279 commands writes command data upward from 0x060E3300, over anything placed in A. The flush then sends those bytes to VDP1 as commands. A longer English Options or text screen drawn through 0x06011344 is a direct way to cause this. The one safe part of A's neighbourhood is at and above 0x060E8000: BUP lib/work at 0x060E8000-0x060EC000+ and the pattern allocator from 0x060E8000 upward are the next users, and neither runs below 0x060E8000. Do not place code in A unless you also add a cap on the command pointer.
A.test: No test is needed to reject A. The flush's own size and high-water code proves the access. To measure how much of the top of A is truly spare: build the English text, run the busiest screens (translated Options, key config, sound test, 2P versus with projectiles on both sides, attract demos, boss fights) with A canary-filled, then read 0x06047D30 and the highest non-0xA5 byte. Any later use of A also needs a patched bound check on 0x060CE668.

B.evidence:
I re-checked the cited points and found no access path.

B's lower edge is the linker end. Crt0 at 0x0600D3B0-0x0600D408, using the tables at 0x06045208 and 0x06047008, clears 0x060CC000-0x060DF784 and 0x060DF784-0x060DF8A8, and copies 0 bytes to 0x060DF8A8. No other code references 0x060DF8A8, so there is no heap above _end.

B's upper edge is a leftover of the boot program. 0.BIN starts with `d002 6f03` and the literal 0x060E1144 is at file offset 0xC, so its entry sets r15 = 0x060E1144. 0.BIN is 271,880 bytes and loads at 0x060A0000-0x060E2608, so B lies inside 0.BIN's own load image. That part of the 0.BIN file (offsets 0x3F8A8-0x40EA4) is all zero. In the dump, the first non-zero byte above 0x060DF8A8 is 0x060E0EA7, which is 0.BIN's stale stack. So B's upper edge is 0.BIN's deepest observed stack use. That matters only while 0.BIN runs, before CYBER.BIN, and any code placed in B would have to be copied in by CYBER.BIN after its crt0 anyway.

No literal in CYBER.BIN or any overlay points into B. The words 0x060E0000 and 0x060E1400 at 0x0604CC90 are data next to a palette table and are never used as pointers. The loader caps of 0x80000 for loads to 0x06060000, 0x06070800 and 0x0608B000 are maximums. The real largest files are STG0AS, ending at 0x060AE4D4, and M?CB*B, ending at most at 0x060A4B3C, so neither reaches B. B is zero in all dumps.

The remaining unknown is the slave SH-2 stack, which the BIOS sets up. The canary would have caught any slave write into B, so this is not a refutation.
B.test: None needed. As an optional check, run one canary pass with a soft reset back to the BIOS and the disc reboot. This confirms that the install code in CYBER.BIN re-copies whatever is placed in B after 0.BIN's stack has touched it again.

C.evidence:
No read or write path reaches C after CYBER.BIN loads, but the last 12 bytes overlap a structure that a pointer refers to. Trim C to 0x06055424-0x06055824 (1,024 bytes).

(1) The overlap. The descriptor at 0x06057044 = {0x06055824, 0x06056824, 0x06057024, 0x0605702C, 0x06057034} (confirmed in the dump), and mech code stores it in object field +52. So 0x06055824 is record 0 of a 16-byte-record table, and its first 12 bytes, 0x06055824-0x0605582F, are inside C. Record 0's remaining bytes (0x06055830 = 00 00 c0 02) are non-zero. All four CYBER readers load the index from byte +102 and branch past the read when it is 0: `tst r4,r4; bt` at 0x060250C2, `tst r5,r5; bt` at 0x060251B0, 0x060251E2 and 0x0602664C. Each then computes @(52,r14) -> @r10 + idx*16, so record 0 is never read by CYBER.BIN. Mech-overlay readers were only sampled.

(2) The table below C. The 4096-byte table at 0x06054424 is indexed at 0x060256CC-0x060256EC as 0x06054424 + row*32 + (rand & 0x1F) with no clamp, and C is exactly rows 128-159. The row is an attack byte (0-2 in the mech tables, or 208 for M?CB06 record 55) plus 10 or a level that is clamped to 0x1F. The reachable rows are therefore at most 33, or 218-239. Rows 218-239 read past C, into the box table at 0x06055C24 and above. No disc data gives a row from 128 to 159.

(3) Loads. C is a run of zero bytes in CYBER.BIN's own file image (offsets 0x48424-0x48830, confirmed all zero), and no other load writes there.
C.test: None needed for 0x06055424-0x06055824. If the last 12 bytes are kept, set a read watchpoint on 0x06055824-0x06055833 during fights with every mech, including M?CB06, and note that mech-overlay readers of field +52 were only sampled.
